projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Helen Shiataku was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: ...interview with Helen Shintaku, a Nisei woman, 80 years old. The interview is being taking place in Long Beach, California, on March the 2nd, 2002. The interviewer is Margo Villanova (ph). Helen, where were you born, and what was the date of your birth?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I was born in Smeltzer, which is not on the map anymore, close to Talbert in Orange County, California, on May the 7th, 1921.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Ah. What was your family's line of work?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My father was a farmer here. In Japan, they had been business people, but he didn't have the...how do you say it? He didn't have the income to start a business, so he went into farming.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Ah. How about your mother? What did she do?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My mother was just a housekeeper here.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How many brothers and sisters did you have?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I had two sisters. We did have one brother who passed away before I was born.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: And do you want to share anything about your family life?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We had a happy family life. We never had much money, but my folks were very good parents.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So you say you were born in Orange County, and I know that you were in LA. When did you move to LA?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: When I was two years old.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: And why did your father move to LA?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My father had been farming when the Santa Ana River flooded -- I forget what year -- but he never could make up the losses. And after I was born, he had three daughters. He'd decided he'd give up on the farming, and we moved to Los Angeles. He started a market, a little store.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, like a grocery store?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Produce, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, that's nice. What schools did you go to?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Went to many grammar schools because whenever the little markets where he was working got competition from larger chains, we would move. So I went to Compton Avenue School, Grant Street School in Hollywood, First Street School. I guess it was just three grammar schools.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. How about high school?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And then junior high, Robert Louis Stevenson Junior High; high school, Roosevelt High School.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Let's see. Is there anything that you want to share about your school years? Any highlights or interesting events that...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I can't think of any interesting events. Talking about schooling and moving, I remember when we first moved to Boyle Heights, and there were many Japanese people there, the girl -- children were speaking to each other in Japanese, and I felt very strange because I didn't feel right speaking Japanese to children. I only spoke it to my parents and not very well at that. And I felt odd speaking English, so I just hardly ever spoke.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. That must have been an adjustment then. Did you encounter any racial prejudice at any time when you were growing up?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Just the one time I remember when a Caucasian friend decided to take us swimming with her children. We went out to, I think it was Riverside, and they refused to let my sister and I go in because we were Japanese.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I was very shocked, but that's the only one I remember.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: You told me about one other time when someone said to you something about...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, in the market when I used to help my parents, I remember one little lady asking me, "Where did you learn to speak such good English?" And as that was the only language I really spoke, you know, it kind of hit me.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: {Giggle} Yeah. Let's move on and talk about, I guess, the beginning of the War. And I want to ask you, how did you hear about Pearl Harbor? What did you feel and think about when that occurred?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: When Pearl Harbor happened, I was in nurse's training near San Diego, and I was naturally stunned when we heard the news. I felt awful. My roommate was also of Japanese descent, and I remember she and I were walking down the street once. And while many people began to try to kind of avoid looking at us or talking to us, the medical director of the hospital crossed the street to where we were just to say hello. And he was a very kind person. That's the main thing I remember then.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. What school was that?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Perez Valley Hospital. It's a Seventh-Day Adventist hospital.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. How old were you at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I was about 20. 19 or 20.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Tell me what happened to you and your family after Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: After Pearl Harbor? Oh. Oh, before we do get to my family, I want to mention one thing. I was passing medications -- I was a medication nurse on the surgical floor at that time...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And the head of that floor was a very kind woman. And she called me over and told me that she just thought I should know that some of the patients were asking weren't they afraid that they would be poisoned by me.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: The patients were saying that?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Some patient ______ --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- but I didn't know who because they were all very nice to my face.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Well, after Pearl Harbor happened, I was worried about where my family would be going. {Clock chimes}

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: It's okay. It's just one time.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh. So I decided to come home and be with them. They had a limit set on the times that we could leave certain areas, so I was in San Diego trying to get home. I went to buy a ticket, and the lady at the counter didn't want to sell me a ticket. She didn't know what was going on apparently and thought that I shouldn't be traveling. So we were holding up a long line of people, and I was getting kind of disgusted with her. And I told her if I had said I was Chinese, you wouldn't have known the difference. So she finally sold me a ticket and I came home.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So she had asked you when you went to the counter if you were Japanese? Is that what she --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, she didn't; she assumed I was.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, she assumed that you were.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, I see. So you finally got your ticket and left?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I came home.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. How did -- how were your family -- how was your family doing, and what did they feel?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My father was quite disappointed. He was very... how do you say? He believed in democracy strongly. And my mother was very upset, And her blood pressure was going way up. And I only had one sister home...oh, that's right. I have another sister who decided that she was going to be separated from her boyfriend because they were moving us to different camps depending on the location we lived. She got married, a very quick marriage, and went off to Manzanar with her husband.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So that left my oldest sister and me and my mother and father.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Did you know like right away, at the time of Pearl Harbor -- when did you first know that they were going to be sending the Japanese people, or the Japanese Americans, away? Was it right away or soon after?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: It wasn't right away. It was maybe a month or two af-...a couple of months after.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I don't remember how I knew.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Just little by little, huh?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So you went to camp. Did you go to an assembly center first?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No. I lived in Boyle Heights. We were sent directly to a relocation camp, as they call it --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- in Poster (ph).

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My sister, however, lived up in Hollywood, and they were sent to Santa Anita Assembly Center.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And then they went to Manzanar.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, wow. Can you tell me a little bit about your life in the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Well, having had some nurse's training, they used us in the medical field. And the hospital was not yet constructed when we moved in. So they assigned one nurse to one doctor. And we covered one quad, which was four blocks, and each block had about 16 barracks, I think. I forget exactly -- 14 or 16. And so I remember trudging over the sand with this doctor. Everybody had diarrhea, of course, at first, the change of the water.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And we didn't have enough paregoric and (Bismuth). He had one (bottle), which is maybe about 20 ounces; I'm not sure. And this doctor that I went with had a very dry sense of humor. Dry. He would ask them, the family, to bring him a little teacup, and he'd pour out a couple spoonfuls of this paregoric for the whole family for their diarrhea.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Laughter} And we'd go the next house that had called.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Nobody had phones, so he was worried about, you know...people would run to you and tell you somebody's sick.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And we need to...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So, about how many people do you think you were responsible for?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Well, there's four quads. At first, I wasn't responsible --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: I mean, but your team?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I don't know. Well, let's see. There were -- most families had four to six in a room. Each barrack had four rooms.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And multiply that by 14, so...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, wow. So that's a lot?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So that's one block. And then we had three other blocks.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Three other blocks.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: You can do the math, I guess. I'll do it later.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Giggle}

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: What did your sister do and what did your parents do while they were in the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My sister had been a seamstress and also an office worker. I think she...I don't even recall what she did at first. But later on, she was working at the clinic after the hospital was established. She worked as a receptionist or something at the clinic. My father later became the block carpentry because he was handy.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: He made the partitions for the women's bathrooms, which they were very grateful for.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Because the toilets were just all in a row.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: You know, it was Army style. And my mother, she suffered a stroke the night before we left.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: She was upset and trying to prepare food for us, and she sort of collapsed at the kitchen sink, and so we did not know what to do with her. She was able to move a little, and we didn't want to leave her with strangers, couldn't get a doctor. So somehow we got her to the...whatever it was that came for us to pick us up to take us to the train, and I must have aged about 10 years that....trying to take care of her because in those days, you know, all we could do was -- they had ice. So I just put cold compresses on her neck and head.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No sphigmom-...you know, we couldn't take her blood pressure. We couldn't do anything.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And when we got there, there was a very kind man named Mr. Evans. He was a dollar-a-year-man volunteer type.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: He took us to our ferry. My mother and I -- and she...I guess after that, she got some medical care from a Dr. Fumicito (ph).

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And her stroke was mild. It was just the left side of her face, and I think her left arm was weak.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So she just stayed in bed for several months, I guess.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: She slowly recovered from that stroke.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. Boy, that must have been a real stressor.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How -- what affect did it have on your family relationships? I mean, clearly what you've said, there was a big change in your relationship to your parents. But how about their relationship to each other and your sister's relationship to you?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I don't think there was any change. We were always a close family.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, that's good. How did you -- what -- can you remember what your feelings were at that time about being put into the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: About being put in, there was so much hysteria in the air that, you know, we just went along with the idea that it would be safer.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: There were many, many people more live...more people lived in the country whose homes were being burned, and where my husband lived in a small town, there was a lot of prejudice. Our -- where we lived in the city, there wasn't that much overt prejudice, but there was still -- we were restricted by different rules that the Government would send out, the Army would say we could go only so many miles from home.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And you couldn't go out after dusk and all that.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So just figured that this was probably the best thing at that time.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. Sort of stepping back, did your parents have to leave their home, or were they able to sell any of it? Did you just leave your things behind?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We took -- you could only take what you could take in your suitcase, so we had to leave the rest behind. Some people were able to leave them with friends and neighbors that would take them.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And some people left them with various organizations, but when they came back, they often were missing, gone.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Can -- were there problems that would arise in the camps other than -- I mean, you've obviously told me of many of the problems that you encountered at the very beginning. How long were you in the camp, and what occurred during that period of time?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I was in camp for one year and three months. By that time, I couldn't wait to get out. Problems that occurred that I recall, there was one big strike that was -- the people of the camp were protesting a case where a couple of the...I forget what they did, but they were going to be sent out of camp to trial. And the people wanted them tried in camp.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So they had a great big strike, and I remember walking with my friend along the -- there was a canal ran through camp. There were on the other side of the canal from the hospital, and we could see all the little campfires because each block had their people out there. They made flags, and they were having a vigil out there.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I don't remember the outcome of that strike, but I do know that -- I think one of the men had beaten up...oh, this is another case; I'm sorry. The people thought this man had sort of betrayed the Japanese people, and they beat him up, and he was brought to the hospital. At that time, I was working nights -- most of the time evenings and nights --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- because we were student nurses. The RNs were fronting on days. And we had charge of everything else in the -- you know, that went on in the evening and the nighttime.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: There was one incident, I remember very well, on a very, very hot day in July, the first year we went -- I went in May. And at that time...I think that was the hottest day we had. I was on the evening shift. Of course, we had no telephones, no gurneys. I was working, and I heard these feet come pounding down the hall, and there was four or six -- I don't know how many men -- carrying the stretcher. They brought in -- it was a workman, a Caucasian workman. He was a very big man. He was DOA. He had had a heat stroke. And shortly after that, here comes this pounding again, and they brought in a young MP, and he was also DOA.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. Oh, my word.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: It was a hot day.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Then I had a death in my ward. A lady who was very ________, and I remember trying to get her bed up and the evening (toys) were coming in. And shortly after that, one of the patients who had had heat exhaustion, a young girl, went into heat stroke, and I sent the orderly running down to hall to get the doctor. And fortunately, we had a good young doctor on, and we were able to save her. But we just poured water over her and on tiles.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And had a fan going on her, and we'd scoop off the water off the mattress as it warmed up.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And poured more over her. But she lived.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yeah. But I'll never forgot that day.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Gosh, that was a lot. That was a lot. Was the doctor --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: It would have been convenient a phone.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Yeah. Was the doctor Japanese?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, yes. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So everybody that kind of was doing all that work was Japanese?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh. The orderlies and nurse's aids were very good. They worked very hard --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- all around the hospital.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. How would you stay in touch with your friends on the outside and your sister, who was in another camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Well, I didn't stay in touch with my friends on the outside. I'd wrote -- I started to write many times to my former roommate, but I was so disgusted by that time, and I just didn't want to send out a letter that sounded --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- like that.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Tear it up. I lost touch with...completely with the people.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, did you?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How about your sister? Are you -- you were able to communicate with her, the one who was in the other camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, yes, we did. Uh-huh. She was in another camp.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Manzanar, and you were --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We could write to each other.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, wow. When you were in the camp, did you kind of look -- try to project forward and see what the end of the tunnel was going to be? Did you kind of imagine what was going to happen after the camp, or...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, I didn't imagine for other people. I guess I just concerned about myself. My friend and I got ahold of a -- some magazine, professional magazine, that listed hospitals and...that had training schools. And, of course, outside of camp, everybody was just crying for nurses.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So we wrote, I think, to over 20 hospitals, and there were only two that were good enough to answer our letters.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And those two, they said they thought we would be happier with those of our own kind.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And so that was the end of that.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: But through...I think it was through the...I don't know who was through (?Walt Indication?) authority or just the head nurse at the hospital, they tried to help us to get out, finish our training.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I didn't stop to consider what would happen to the people afterwards.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Oh, I mean, yeah. You would only think about yourself and what would happen.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So you just thought, well, I want to get out and finish my training --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: -- so I could be a registered nurse.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: But I did -- I do remember standing at the window, we had -- we were in the dormitory because they wanted nursing and doctors to be close by. Of course, you'd have to run over to their house to get them out of the place.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Across the firebreak, I could see the camp and black tar-paper-covered barracks and brown roofs. It was so depressing to look at. And I'd stand there and think about all these people whose lives were uprooted, and I gradually became pretty depressed.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Did you? How about your father? Was he depressed as well or...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, I don't think so. He was disappointed, but he would stand up to some of the other more radical people who were --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- talking down America and so forth.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And he would tell them that if the situation were reversed and he -- you know, they were prisoners of war with Japan, they wouldn't be fed this well --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- or treated this well.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: I know that...kind of moving forward a little bit, You met your husband while you were in the camp. Can you tell me a little bit about how you met him and...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: He came to work at the hospital as an ambulance driver after he was fired as a truck driver. He had been driving a...what they call a water truck, watering the roads, and he got to wandering around too much for the supervisors. They didn't like the idea that he was going off. He wanted to see what was around there. So he just, you know, had the opportunity and drove around until they got fired, and he came to work as an ambulance driver.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And he was originally from San Juan Bautista. So this is one thing that happened that, I guess, was good. I would never have met him otherwise.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. So how did your relationship progress, and did you do anything for fun? Did you go on a date with him? {Giggle}

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: For fun, we took walks in the desert when it wasn't too hot.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: That was it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: They did have block dances, some blocks.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: But, of course, we worked evenings and nights so...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Rarely off.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Were there any recreational activities in the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: They had movies. They had some different movies brought in.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And outdoor -- outdoor, in-the-open-air movies. But I don't recall -- I think there were many little sports groups that came up.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I didn't work in that recreation area, so I don't know much about what they did.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Oh, because you were busy taking care of the people.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We were very busy.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: If it wasn't for that, I probably would have gotten much more depressed.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Yeah. I would imagine so. It's amazing. So did you get married while you were in the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, I left finally. I was accepted at the Episcopal Hospital in Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Philadelphia, and I went there and started training again. And my husband talked three of his friends into coming out there too, and they went -- they got jobs in Philadelphia. And then the Army was about to take him as a replacement for the...what was it? The 100th, or the 442nd?

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Yeah. I don't remember the --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: There were many casualties.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And they were giving them a very short training and sending them over, so I decided that...we decided to get married. And to get married, we moved back to Denver?

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I left the nurse's training.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And we were married in Denver.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And from there, he was inducted at Jefferson Barracks together --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- with my sister's husband.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Hmm. When you were out then, were your parents still in the camp at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, they were.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Were you able to communicate with them?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, yeah...well, by mail.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: By mail.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How did they feel about your getting married?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I guess they were...I guess they were happy for me. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I didn't...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: I guess if they were unhappy, you would have known.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So you and your sister were in Denver together then?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Your older sister?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes. She's two years older than I am.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Ah. Well, that's nice. When your husbands went away, did you and your sister stay together?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yeah, we did for a little while. We were there -- I was trying to get my husband's folks out of camp, and I had found a place for them to live in Denver. And I went down to the (postman) to see about getting them up there. The doctor told me that my father-in-law's heart was in no condition to -- for that altitude. So I went on to Los Angeles, and we found something...I found sort of a temporary place for them to live there, and I had a promise of a job. So I went back to Denver. My sister and I came to Los Angeles together. And at that time, there was no housing anywhere in LA. You know, it was wartime.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We had rations and so forth and so on. So we couldn't find a place to sleep that first night. We kept trying the "Y" and different places, and I was ready to sleep at the Union Station when my sister tried the YWCA [sic] one more time. And they said yes, we can come in for one night. So we went there.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And then through the papers, we found a job for her. We found housing for us. There was a lady that wanted... had a duplex and was willing to let us live in one side in exchange for doing the housework for her.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And since I already had been promised a job as an infant nurse, my sister got the job of taking care of the house for the lady.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. That sounds like it was quite an adventure.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Giggle} Yes, it was -- it would have been adventurous to sleep at the Union Station, I think.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Yeah. Now, what year was this that you were out of the camp and you had had some more training, when you came back to LA? What year was that, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I think it was '45.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Was the war still going on at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Was the War over?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: It was over then?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: '45, '46. I forget. I don't remember what month we came, but I was driving across...in a bus going across Texas after I saw my husband. And that was VJD [sic], I think that happened, so it was after that.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How did you feel? You were in Texas on VJ-Day?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I was on a bus, yes. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. What was that like?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, people were just happy. And I really...I guess I was happy about it, but, you know, you were kind of numb.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah. But nobody -- when you were doing all this traveling, did you ever have bad experiences with people or...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No. I had a good experience with a man when I was going from...I guess I was going from Denver to Texas to see my husband, and we had been talking. He was in the seat behind me, and I fell asleep. I guess that must have been a pretty empty train because I had took two seats to myself.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And when I woke up, the man had covered me with his coat.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, that was kind of nice, huh?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, that was very nice. No, I didn't have any unpleasant experiences.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, that's good. I'm going to put this on pause...{Tape paused} Helen, can you tell me some more things about your life in the camp, some feelings of prejudice that you might have had?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes. I think gradually I became more and more depressed about the situation, being stuck in that camp, all the people in camp.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And so when any little incident happened, it would sort of be exacerbated in my mind, I guess. There was one nurse that -- a Caucasian nurse, that the -- nobody wanted, I guess, on the outside. So she was there because there was a shortage of nurses outside. But she was stealing milk from the nursery refrigerator. At that time, there wasn't enough milk for the children, but there was milk for the babies. And she was drinking it, and that upset me very much. Also, whenever we had a Caucasian teacher or somebody that was sick with, say, an earache --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- and they would put her in a private room because they were fearful that the rest of the patients...

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: ...where we really needed that room for somebody that was acutely ill.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Those kind of things would get me. Gradually, I was getting kind of...how do you say...angry, I guess, at everybody that -- any little thing that happened.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: We had a polio outbreak in camp. And at that time, I was on...I forget which ward it was, medical, surgical, or something, but this was on night shift. There was...I guess they had about ten patients there. And nurses' aids were covering the night shift.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: There was an excellent nurse's aid that was taking care of the patients when in charge of it. She was a little older. Then it happened that the Camp Two administrator got polio. And so when he came in as a patient, they assigned me to that ward again. And I was quite angry because to me it seemed that they didn't care who took care of the inmates.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: But if a Caucasian person came in, they had to have somebody with some kind of a title behind them.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I was so upset that I didn't go in to see him the first night I was there. She was a good nurse's aid. I'd figured she'd been taking care of him, and I just couldn't face him because I wasn't up to it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: The next day I did. I did go in and see him and took care of him. And I feel very badly about not being able to take care of him the first day, but I was too angry.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I guess that's about it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Sounds like it was a very hard training...{Laughter}...in dealing...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Laughter} It was a great experience, I guess.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Well, it was experience; that's for sure. So when did you parents leave the camp?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: They left about the time camp was closed. I forget when that was. '46.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I'm not sure.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: And did they join you at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No. My sister and her husband came out, and they found them a place.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: They found a house in the city, in Boyle Heights.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Ah. And how were your parents? What was their transition back to life, a free life? Do you remember anything about their reactions and when they came back?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, I don't really. You know, my mother was better by then.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: You know, she was recovered mostly from her stroke. And my father, (in) business concern, was probably getting some work. He worked all his life, and he did find a job in the celery shoots. I think there were quite a few people that were hired. But I don't know what they (do), packing celery.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: That sounds like might have been hard work.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Sort of, but he was used to it. He used to grow celery in Orange County.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, uh-huh. Wow.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So he was familiar with that.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you have trouble finding a job after the War?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No, because of the fact that I had had some nurse's training.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I went to work as an infant nurse for some very wonderful Jewish people.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. Uh-huh. Was that like a private -- in a private home? Is that --

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: -- what you mean by infant nurse?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I lived in.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And the lady was a buyer for May Company, and the husband and his brother-in-law probably {Clock chimes} were in construction.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Hmm. How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I guess about a year. I forget.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. And then during that time, did your husband come back from the service?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: My husband was discharged, and I left there.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And I remember this Jewish lady talking to me one time about how she was traveling to New York and talking to a woman. They were having a nice conversation until this lady brought up this, "Now we have this Jewish problem." And she told the lady, "I'm Jewish, and I've never considered myself a problem."

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: {Laughter} But they were very nice people.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Were they?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh, that's nice. {Tape paused and restarted} _______ We're wrapping up now. Have you -- did you discuss your experiences with your children?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, my husband and I both did. We talked a lot about what went on in camp and various things like that, and my husband has a very good memory about everything that happened in camp and before camp. My friend, that I mentioned walked along the canal with me when the strike was on, she was a student nurse from Phoenix.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: She was not there too long, but she left everything out because many times...I've seen her since then, and I mention, do you remember when we did this? No, she doesn't remember.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And she recently called me and asked me about the camps because her grandson was supposed to write a paper about it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: And she had no recollection of much of it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Wow. That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: A lot of people did block it out, I guess --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- and they didn't talk about it.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: How about you and your parents? You said you spoke with your children about it. Did you and your parents talk about the experience?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, yes. Well, not a lot, but then it was not something that we buried.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. And you had already said that you didn't really have a problem getting a job, and you were able to go out and...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Uh-huh. Oh, before the camps, though, we had problems. When I tried to get into nursing school, there was prejudice against Japanese --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- and Jews. And I applied to most of the schools in the LA area, and I was refused by most of them. The only ones that would accept me were the Seventh-Day Adventist, a couple of Catholic schools, and the...what is it? State colleges.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: This is before the War?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, before the War.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: So this was prejudice even before the War started?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Oh, yes, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Oh. Hmm.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: So I guess we sort of built a shell and, you know, brush it off as you get older.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Don't think about it. But you were traveling across country. When you went across the country to the nursing school in Philadelphia, were you by yourself?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes, I was. But I was accustomed to riding streetcars in Los Angeles, and it didn't bother me at all.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh. Wow. And you said that it was -- the Government paid your way to go to Philadelphia to...

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: Yes. And so I figured as long as they're paying my way, I'd see as much of the country as I could. I had been accepted --

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: -- in Chicago, but...{laughter}...I thought Philadelphia was further east.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: That's a better choice...{laughter}...as far as I'm concerned. Philadelphia is my hometown.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: People there were very friendly.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: I had never met that type of friendliness out here in California. We were just sort of accepted on the surface anyhow.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: But in Philadelphia, if you stood on the street corner and looked around, somebody would come up and ask if they could help you.

sp.speaker: Margo Villanova
sp.p: Hmm. As we get towards the end, are there some things that you would like to sum up or anything else that you want to bring in or share with us that we didn't cover while we were talking?

sp.speaker: Helen Shiataku
sp.p: No. The only thing that I would share is that this type of thing should never happen. It happened once; it should never happen again. That's all.
